articles.title: Heathland plan to support two rare species of ant
articles.summary: Devon Wildlife Trust says it will improve the heathland homes of the narrow-headed and erratic ants.
articles.content:
Two of the UK's rarest ant species are being supported by a new conservation project.

Chiefs at Devon Wildlife Trust said they plan to improve the heathland homes of both the narrow-headed and erratic ants, and start new colonies at suitable nearby sites.

The only English population of the narrow-headed ant lives in the trust's Chudleigh Knighton Heath nature reserve and the nationally scarce erratic ant was recently discovered at the charity's Bovey Heathfield nature reserve.

The three-year project by the wildlife trust and invertebrate conservation charity Buglife has been funded with £212,000 from the government's wildlife restoration campaign.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a funded conservation project aimed at protecting and expanding populations of two rare ant species in the UK, which has meaningful environmental and biodiversity benefits with a clear scope and positive real-world impact.
articles.personality_title: Devon Wildlife Trust launches project to protect rare ants
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Two rare ant species, the narrow-headed and erratic ants, live in special heathland areas in Devon, England. These ants are very uncommon and need help to survive.

**What happened** – Devon Wildlife Trust, together with Buglife, an insect conservation group, started a three-year project to improve the ants’ heathland homes. They will also create new colonies nearby. The narrow-headed ant lives only at Chudleigh Knighton Heath, while the erratic ant was recently found at Bovey Heathfield. The project is supported by £212,000 from the government’s wildlife restoration campaign.

**Impact** – This project is important because it helps protect two of the UK’s rarest ants by improving and expanding their living areas. By creating new colonies, the ants have a better chance to grow and survive. This work also helps keep the heathland ecosystem healthy, which benefits many other plants and animals.

**What's next step** – Over the next three years, the teams will work on the land to make it better for the ants and monitor how the colonies grow. If successful, this project could be a model for helping other rare insects in the UK.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new project in Devon is improving homes and creating new colonies for two rare ant species to help them survive and thrive in the wild.

articles.title: Mysteries of the deep and AI friendship: Books in brief
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02725-9Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.
articles.content:
When the Forest Breathes Suzanne Simard Knopf (2026)

In 2015, forest ecologist Suzanne Simard established the Mother Tree Project in British Columbia, Canada, funded by the country’s federal government. Now, Simard and her team, aided by local Indigenous people, have planted 225,000 trees across an area as large as Denmark, including in both the province’s rugged interior and the lush rainforests on its west coast. Their goals are “to document the effects of clearcut logging on carbon pools and biodiversity” and “to discover new ways of tending forests”, which she discusses in her appealing book.

The Unconscious Antonio Melechi MIT Press (2026)

Any book on the history of the unconscious mind has to accept that the topic has always been rife with disagreement. “Inside the conceptual rubric of ‘the unconscious’ we find a babel of confusion and disputation,” observes Antonio Melechi, a historian of medicine and psychology. His complex book includes extracts from numerous eras and sources, from Hippocrates to Charles Darwin and Sigmund Freud, although he oddly omits biophysicist Francis Crick’s study of consciousness, The Astonishing Hypothesis (1994).

The Dark Frontier Jeffrey Marlow Random House (2026)

The deep sea — which begins at a depth of around 200 metres, where light from the surface cannot reach — accounts for more than 95% of Earth’s habitable volume. Yet scientists have seen less than 0.001% of the deep sea’s floor and even less of the water column above it, according to biologist Jeffrey Marlow. His outstanding portrait of the deep ocean considers its role in “sustaining a viable planet and a thriving human civilization”, despite humanity’s tendency to pollute and damage the sea “before even getting to know it”.

Artificially Yours Valerie Tiberius Princeton Univ. Press (2026)
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant environmental initiative, the Mother Tree Project, which involves large-scale reforestation efforts in British Columbia with measurable benefits for carbon sequestration and biodiversity. It also discusses scientific exploration of the deep sea, emphasizing its crucial role in sustaining the planet and human civilization, which is inspiring and impactful for society at large.
articles.personality_title: Canada’s Mother Tree Project and deep sea research highlight nature’s hidden power
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Forests and oceans play key roles in keeping our planet healthy, but human activities have harmed these natural places. Scientists are working to understand and protect them better.

**What happened** – In British Columbia, Canada, forest ecologist Suzanne Simard started the Mother Tree Project in 2015. With help from Indigenous communities, her team has planted 225,000 trees across an area as big as Denmark. They study how cutting down trees affects carbon storage and wildlife, and look for better ways to care for forests. Meanwhile, biologist Jeffrey Marlow wrote about the deep sea, which is mostly unexplored and very important for life on Earth. He explains how the deep ocean helps support the planet and people, even though it is often polluted.

**Impact** – The Mother Tree Project is one of the biggest reforestation efforts in Canada, showing how teamwork and science can help recover forests. This helps slow climate change by storing carbon and protects many plants and animals. Learning more about the deep sea reminds us that much of Earth’s life is still unknown and worth protecting. These projects together highlight important steps to understand and care for nature.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue planting trees and studying the forest’s health to find the best ways to protect it over time. Deep sea scientists will keep exploring and monitoring ocean health to better understand its role and how to reduce pollution. These efforts can guide future actions to protect the environment.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Large-scale tree planting in Canada and new deep ocean research show how science helps us protect vital natural systems that support life on Earth.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le projet Mother Tree au Canada et la recherche sur les abysses révèlent la puissance cachée de la nature

articles.title: Climate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
articles.summary: As rising temperatures reshape France's vineyards, winemakers are turning to Normandy and Brittany, regions once known for cider, not grapes. Those fleeing harsher conditions in traditional areas like the Loire Valley see opportunity up north, though some warn the same climate volatility disrupting southern vineyards is starting to follow them there.
articles.content:
In a green valley in Normandy, rows of grapevines stretch across slopes where an apple orchard once stood.

In a land long associated with cider and Calvados, winemaker Sebastien Fricker is betting that a warming climate can turn one of France's northernmost regions into its newest wine country.

"These days, to have a fine vineyard and good grapes, you really need a stable climate from spring right through to autumn," said Fricker. "And at the moment, Normandy is very well suited to that."

The heir to five generations of winemakers in the Loire Valley left his family's historic wine-growing region in central France as climate change and worsening soil quality made growing conditions increasingly challenging.

"I really couldn't see myself taking on another vineyard in the Loire," the 36-year-old said.

"That's what led me to Normandy. I thought: perhaps it's time to take a step back and consider what the next 50 years of viticulture might look like."

In 2020, Fricker settled on four hectares of land in a village in the Calvados department, about a 30-minute drive from the seaside resort of Deauville. He now grows two white and two red grape varieties, including Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon.

Successive heatwaves, compounded by wildfires and drought, disrupted life for France's winegrowers. © Romain Perrocheau, AFP

He chose the village of Marolles for the quality of its terroir, its clay-limestone soil and a stable climate with few thunderstorms and limited temperature variations.

Even in late August, despite recent extreme heat, the vegetation remained green here.

Read moreFontainebleau forest near Paris reopens after devastating wildfire

This year, successive heatwaves, wildfires and drought, disrupted life for France's winegrowers, leading to historically early harvests, lower yields, and an increased risk of smoke taint.

'New wine regions'

Fricker believes climate change will inevitably reshape France's wine map.

In recent years, vineyards have been expanding into Normandy, Brittany and Hauts-de-France, France's northernmost region, long associated with grey skies, rain and blustery weather rather than wine production.

Winegrowers believe that climate change will inevitably reshape France's wine map. © Sébastien Salom-Gomis, AFP

"We will no longer be able to produce solely in the south," Fricker said.

For now the output remains negligible.

Normandy has around 20 producers cultivating 20 hectares, compared with 85,000 hectares in the southwestern region of Bordeaux.

Together they produce fewer than 100,000 bottles a year.

Maxime Gazeau of the Norman Winegrowers' Union (SyViNor) said almost all locally made wine is sold directly by producers.

"We have no problem selling our wine," he said, adding that the main challenge remained producing "high-quality wine".

Vine planting is strictly regulated in the European Union. While climate change has made vine-growing more viable in northern France, industry experts say its spread has also been aided by an EU reform that eased vine-planting rules in 2016.

French winemaker Marina Fourrure said Brittany was 'now a very good place to plant vines'. © Sébastien Salom-Gomis, AFP

Among those to benefit were Marina and Loic Fourrure, who have been cultivating six hectares of vines in Theix-Noyalo in the northwestern region of Brittany since 2021, with an inlet and marshes the backdrop to their vineyard.

"Brittany is now a very good place to plant vines," said Marina Fourrure, hard at work harvesting her plots during an exceptionally early vintage.

'Mind-blowing'

She said winegrowers from the south had told her and her husband they were right to be growing grapes in Brittany and complained that extreme weather was disrupting vine growth and driving up alcohol levels.

"Sugar levels are getting far too high, they need to find solutions, but perhaps the pleasure has gone out of it," said the winemaker.

Climate disruption could also be felt in Brittany, she said.

Read moreWinemakers across Europe face the challenges of climate change

"There are no upsides to global warming," she added.

Her husband, Loic Fourrure, chimed in.

"We've had frosts, droughts and excessive rain. And we are harvesting on August 22," he said. "It's properly mind-blowing."

Loic Fourrure said they managed to demonstrate that winegrowing in Brittany has 'potential for the future'. © Sébastien Salom-Gomis, AFP

At the same time he said they had managed to demonstrate that winegrowing in Brittany has "potential for the future".

Loic Fourrure is co-president of the Breton Winegrowers' Association that represents some 50 estates spanning around 160 hectares.

But he warned that establishing vineyards was a long-term effort.

"To call it a winegrowing El Dorado would be going a bit too far," he said.

"It will be another 20 years before our vines are fully mature and capable of producing really fine grapes."

Vineyards in the Hauts-de-France region, which lies along the English Channel, now cover approximately 130 hectares, estimated Bruno Cardot, a local winegrower.

"Today we have the climate that the Champagne wine region had in the 1970s," he said.

"Climate change is clearly pushing all kinds of agriculture, including viticulture, northwards in France," he added.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the positive adaptation of French winemakers to climate change by expanding vineyards into northern regions like Normandy and Brittany, demonstrating a tangible response to environmental challenges with broad agricultural and economic implications. articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: Ice Island Survives Run-In With Joe Island
articles.summary: In summer 2026, a substantial iceberg calved from Petermann Glacier in northwest Greenland and swiftly drifted into Nares Strait, colliding with an island along the way.
articles.content:
AUGUST 24 AUGUST 23 A satellite view shows the iceberg after it pivoted out of the fjord into Nares Strait, wedged against a small, brown island. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A satellite view shows a large tabular iceberg at the junction of its home fjord and Nares Strait. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin AUGUST 24 AUGUST 23 A satellite view shows the iceberg after it pivoted out of the fjord into Nares Strait, wedged against a small, brown island. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A satellite view shows a large tabular iceberg at the junction of its home fjord and Nares Strait. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin AUGUST 24 AUGUST 23 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details An iceberg from Petermann Glacier encounters Joe Island in northwestern Greenland, visible in images captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on August 23, 2026 (right), and August 24, 2026 (left). NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin.

Summer is prime iceberg season in Greenland’s glacier-fed fjords, and 2026 was no exception. Especially notable was the berg that broke from the Petermann Glacier along Greenland’s northwest coast in August. Roughly the size of St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands, it was the largest calving event by any Arctic glacier since 2020.

Iceberg calving is a routine part of an outlet glacier’s life cycle. Scientists watch the process closely, however, along with numerous other observations of the ice and its environment, for longer-term signs of instability. Petermann is one of Greenland's largest marine-terminating glaciers and acts as a gatekeeper for ice flowing from the ice sheet into the ocean. Its future stability has implications for sea level rise.

The calving event of summer 2026 was spotted on August 4 by Adam Garbo, a doctoral student in glaciology at the University of Ottawa, in imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 mission. Garbo and an international team of colleagues have been using remote sensing to study and track the glacier's ice tongue.

The team reported that the large tabular iceberg, or “ice island,” measured just over 76 square kilometers (29 square miles) at the time it calved—the largest to break from the glacier since the ice island of 2012 (130 square kilometers). The 2012 calving followed earlier major events in 2008 (31 square kilometers) and 2010 (just over 250 square kilometers).

The August 2026 event could have been even bigger. Garbo and colleagues had been expecting a major calving once one of the large rifts they were monitoring finally cut all the way across Petermann’s ice tongue. “What surprised us was that the calving instead followed a different fracture, producing a smaller ice island than we had originally anticipated,” Garbo said. As of late August, two large rifts remained and were expected to eventually produce new ice islands of roughly 94 square kilometers and 84 square kilometers, though the timing remained uncertain.

August 24, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College has also been tracking the iceberg, using images from NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, as it drifted down Petermann Fjord toward Nares Strait. In the week since it calved, the berg drifted an average of 3 kilometers per day. It continued toward the fjord’s junction with Nares Strait, where it rammed into a small rocky outcrop known as Joe Island (Joe Ø). The brief encounter is visible in images captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on August 23 (top right) and August 24 (top left). A detailed view of the August 24 image is shown above.

Joe Island sits at the mouth of Petermann Fjord, making it one of the first obstacles a departing ice island meets. Collisions with it—like the one that split the 2010 ice island in two—often mark the start of a berg’s breakup. Petermann bergs tend to be thinner and more fragile than those calved by glaciers such as Greenland’s Jakobshavn and Helheim, and thinner still than Antarctica’s behemoths, Pelto noted.

“We were certainly watching closely as it interacted with Joe Island and were impressed that it survived the interaction without further fragmentation,” Garbo said.

The ice island was estimated to be less than 150 meters thick at the time of calving. Wind and surface currents have swept it out of the fjord, and satellite images show it pivoting away from Joe Island and continuing southwest through Nares Strait. As it drifts, it will fracture into smaller pieces as tides, winds, currents, and melting continue to weaken the ice.

Thicker bergs that calve from tidewater glaciers without floating ice-shelf extensions can drag and even become grounded on the seafloor within the fjord, while ice islands, like those from Petermann, might run aground later in their drift. Many ice islands have become "grounded" off the coasts of Coburg and Baffin islands.

Garbo and colleagues noted that ice islands and their fragments have been known to travel considerable distances, posing potential hazards to marine activities and infrastructure while also distributing freshwater through the ocean as they melt.
